item.title: Scattered Spider Attribution, Januscape KVM Escape, and AI Platform Isolation Flaws
item.content:encoded:
UAT-7810 continues building ORB networks using new malware — Must Read

Cisco Talos reports that China-nexus actor UAT-7810 is expanding the LapDogs Operational Relay Box network by exploiting unpatched routers and deploying new custom malware including LONGLEASH, DOGLEASH, JARLEASH, and LEASHTEST. The activity shows continued development of relay infrastructure likely used by other China-nexus APTs to target high-value victims.

  • Cisco Talos is tracking infrastructure and malware associated with UAT-7810, a China-nexus threat actor responsible for maintaining and expanding the LapDogs Operational Relay Box network.
  • Talos assesses that UAT-7810 is most likely tasked with establishing Operational Relay Box networks that can be leveraged by associated secondary threat actors for malicious attacks against high-value targets.
  • UAT-7810 continues to develop its custom SHORTLEASH malware, with Talos tracking a newer version as LONGLEASH.
  • Talos discovered two new malware families in UAT-7810's arsenal: DOGLEASH, a C-based backdoor for compromised Linux devices, and JARLEASH, a Java-based backdoor used for administration purposes.
  • Talos observed UAT-7810 primarily exploiting known vulnerabilities in unpatched Ruckus wireless routers, including CVE-2020-22653, CVE-2020-22658, and CVE-2023-25717.

New Januscape Linux flaw allows VM escape on Intel, AMD devices — Must Read

A 16-year-old Linux KVM flaw called Januscape lets attackers with root access inside a guest VM escape to the host and potentially take over or crash all VMs on the same machine. KVM/x86 hosts, especially multi-tenant cloud systems, should ensure the June 2026 kernel patch is applied.

  • A 16-year-old Linux kernel vulnerability dubbed Januscape, tracked as CVE-2026-53359, allows attackers to escape a virtual machine and execute arbitrary code on the host.
  • The flaw stems from a use-after-free weakness in the shadow MMU emulation of KVM/x86 and was patched in June 2026.
  • Successful exploitation requires root access inside a guest virtual machine and can let attackers execute code as root on the host or crash the host kernel.
  • Hyunwoo Kim said Januscape is the first guest-to-host exploit that can be triggered on both Intel and AMD processor architectures.
  • Administrators running KVM/x86 hosts that accept multi-tenant guests should confirm that patch commit 81ccda30b4e8 has been applied to the host kernel.

Fake Installers, Fake Reviews, Fake Services – Real Proxies, Real Victims — Should Read

Infoblox researchers link the fake 7-Zip installer campaign to a years-long operation called Lurking Lizard that uses lookalike domains, trojanized apps, and fake proxy services to turn victims’ devices into residential proxy nodes. The activity appears to span multiple brands including WireVPN and is tied together by shared infrastructure, telemetry, and domain registration patterns.

  • Infoblox tracks the actor as Lurking Lizard and says it used fake 7-Zip installers hosted at 7zip[.]com to enroll victim devices as proxy nodes for residential proxy services.
  • DNS and infrastructure analysis identified more than 230 domains tied to the operation, including lookalike domains impersonating software, VPNs, virtual phone number services, and proxy providers such as IPIDEA, SmartProxy, IP Royal, and 911Proxy.
  • A hardcoded IPLogger URL found in multiple samples linked the fake 7-Zip campaign to other payloads dating back to at least 2022, including video downloader malware and WireVPN-themed variants.
  • The newer WireVPN samples showed similarities to the earlier 7-Zip-related payloads, including comparable file names, installation paths, firewall rule creation with netsh, service-style execution, and persistence through registry modifications.
  • Infoblox assessed that Lurking Lizard operates a broader residential proxy ecosystem that includes victim acquisition, proxy infrastructure, lookalike proxy service brands, and fake review sites used for marketing and monetization.

Rogue Agent: How a Single Code Block Could Hijack Your AI Conversations in Google’s DialogFlow — Should Read

Varonis found a critical flaw in Google Dialogflow CX that let anyone with a single playbook update permission inject persistent code into the shared Code Blocks execution environment, enabling silent conversation hijacking, data exfiltration, phishing, and VPC-SC bypass across agents in the same GCP project. Google has patched the issue, and customers should review Dialogflow playbook update logs and Code Blocks for signs of abuse.

  • Varonis Threat Labs discovered a critical vulnerability in Google Cloud Platform’s Dialogflow CX service and named it Rogue Agent.
  • The vulnerability allowed attackers with the dialogflow.playbooks.update permission on one agent to use Playbook Code Blocks to inject persistent malicious code into the Dialogflow agents’ pipeline.
  • Attackers could exfiltrate conversation data, manipulate chatbot responses, and run phishing prompts disguised as legitimate agent messages.
  • The issue affected Dialogflow CX agents with Playbook Code Blocks before Google issued an initial security update in April 2026 and fully resolved it in June 2026.
  • Varonis and Google recommend that customers audit Dialogflow CX configurations for suspicious Playbook updates and analyze past playbook update actions.

Court Filing Reveals Windows Device ID Helped FBI Trace Alleged Scattered Spider Hacker — Should Read

A newly unsealed complaint says the FBI traced alleged Scattered Spider member Peter Stokes to a 2025 jewelry retailer breach using a persistent Windows device ID linked to accounts and travel records. The case highlights both the group’s help-desk social engineering tactics and why arresting one operator may not significantly slow the broader, loosely organized threat.

  • U.S. prosecutors linked alleged Scattered Spider hacker Peter Stokes to a May 2025 intrusion at a luxury jewelry retailer using a persistent Windows Global Device Identifier from Microsoft records.
  • Attackers called the retailer’s IT help desk from Google Voice numbers, impersonated locked-out employees, and obtained password and multifactor authentication resets for three accounts, including two IT administrator accounts.
  • During the intrusion, the attackers installed ngrok and Teleport, moved data to Amazon cloud storage, and stole at least 77 gigabytes of data before the retailer blocked an apparent ransomware deployment attempt.
  • The attackers demanded $8 million in cryptocurrency, the company did not pay, and the breach cost about $2 million in disruption, investigation, and cleanup.
  • The article states that Scattered Spider is described by Group-IB as a loose collective of small independent cells, meaning individual arrests may not stop the broader threat.

Writer AI Flaw Could Let Agent Previews Leak Session Tokens Across Tenants — Should Read

Researchers disclosed a now-patched Writer AI flaw, dubbed WriteOut, that let attackers use a malicious agent preview link to steal logged-in users’ session tokens across tenants. The issue could have allowed account takeover and access to private enterprise chats, documents, agents, configurations, models, connectors, and credentials.

  • Cybersecurity researchers disclosed a now-patched critical session isolation vulnerability in Writer, an enterprise generative AI platform, that could enable cross-tenant compromise.
  • Sand Security Research codenamed the one-click vulnerability WriteOut and said an outsider could take over any Writer AI organization with only a link.
  • An attacker could create an agent in their own Writer account, share a public live preview link, and steal the session token of a logged-in Writer user who opened it.
  • The stolen session token could let the attacker take over the victim’s Writer account and access private chats, documents, agents, configurations, private models, connectors, and LLM credentials.
  • Writer addressed the issue by preventing user session cookies from being forwarded into sandbox previews and moving previews to an isolated origin.

UK cyber pledge draws only a handful of top firms despite ministerial appeal — May Read

The UK government’s voluntary Cyber Resilience Pledge launched with limited backing from major companies, with fewer than 15 of the FTSE 350 signing up despite direct ministerial appeals. The weak response may strengthen the case for future mandatory cybersecurity regulation.

  • Fewer than 15 of Britain’s 350 largest listed companies signed the UK government’s voluntary Cyber Resilience Pledge at its launch, despite ministers writing to every FTSE 350 chair and chief executive eight months earlier.
  • The launch named 70 founding signatories, including 20 strategic government suppliers invited through a separate Government Cyber Charter.
  • The pledge asks signatories to make cybersecurity a board-level responsibility, register for the National Cyber Security Centre’s free Early Warning service, and take a risk-based approach to requiring Cyber Essentials certification across supply chains.
  • The pledge remains voluntary and has no enforcement mechanism, while the government said it will review the pledge’s suitability and may refine its actions after a 12-month cycle.
  • Jamie MacColl of the Royal United Services Institute said the low number of signatories could fit a UK cyber policy pattern of voluntary measures preceding regulation.

The Name You Trust, the Domain You've Never Seen: A Photo Lure That Passed Every Auth Check — May Read

A phishing email impersonated a trusted colleague by using their display name while sending from an unrelated but fully authenticated domain, allowing SPF, DKIM, and DMARC to pass. The real warning signs were the sender-name mismatch and a same-day-registered photo-link domain, showing that authentication alone cannot prove an email is safe.

  • An attacker sent a phishing email that displayed the name of a trusted colleague while actually originating from the unrelated external address noreply@unrelated-domain[.]es.
  • The email passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC authentication checks, demonstrating that these controls confirmed the sending domain but not whether the display name honestly represented the sender.
  • The lure used a short personal note offering two photos and included a single unfamiliar link to hxxps://sxzqw[.]eszdgwbtsr[.]com/.
  • A WHOIS lookup showed that eszdgwbtsr[.]com was created on June 17, 2026, the same day the email was delivered, and was registered behind a privacy service.
  • The platform quarantined the message automatically after detecting the display-name mismatch, the unfamiliar same-day domain, and phishing-like language patterns before any recipient clicked the link.

Threat landscape for industrial automation systems. Q1 2026 — Optional

Kaspersky reports that the share of ICS computers where malicious objects were blocked fell to a three-year low of 19.6% in Q1 2026, though internet-sourced threats rose slightly. Biometric systems remained the most affected sector, while Southern Europe, Russia, and Southeast Asia saw notable increases in specific threat categories.

  • The percentage of ICS computers on which malicious objects were blocked continued to decrease in Q1 2026, reaching 19.6%, the lowest value in three years.
  • Regional percentages of attacked ICS computers ranged from 9.1% in Northern Europe to 27.4% in Africa, with increases over the quarter in five regions including Southern Europe, Northern Europe, and Russia.
  • Biometric systems ranked highest among the selected industries and OT infrastructure types, with malicious objects blocked on 26.4% of ICS computers in that category.
  • Kaspersky security solutions blocked malware from 10,052 different malware families on industrial automation systems in Q1 2026.
  • Internet threats were the only main threat source whose global average increased in Q1 2026, rising to 7.88%, while email, removable media, and network folder threat percentages decreased.

Crime and Punishment in the Russian-Speaking Cybercriminal Underground — Optional

The article examines how Russian-speaking cybercriminal forums police their own communities, using reputation systems, arbitration, bans, and public shaming to manage scams and disputes in an otherwise illegal marketplace.

  • The article examines how Russian-speaking cybercriminal communities handle wrongdoing within their own underground forums and marketplaces.
  • The article describes reputation, trust, and dispute resolution as important mechanisms in these criminal communities.
  • The article explains that members who scam or violate community rules can face consequences such as public accusations, bans, or loss of status.
  • The article frames these internal rules as a way for illegal marketplaces to keep functioning despite being built around criminal activity.

What Changes When Your Software Supply Chain Includes AI Writing Your Code? — Optional

AI coding agents are becoming part of the software supply chain, so security programs must track and govern models, agents, prompts, and tools—not just scan the code they produce. The key takeaway is that provenance and exploitability-based prioritization need to extend across the entire AI-enabled build pipeline.

  • AI tools, models, and related infrastructure have become important parts of how software is built, deployed, and run.
  • The article argues that AI-generated code should not be treated only as more code to scan because risk now also applies to the model, agent, and tooling behind the artifact.
  • The article says prompts can be used as inputs to the build process and may steer what code gets written or what dependencies are pulled in.
  • The article states that software supply chain security programs need lineage that covers models and agents as well as code and other dependencies.
  • The article says prioritization should be based on real exploitability and runtime context rather than simply adding more findings to already overloaded queues.

Unveiling Silent Push 6.0: MCP Server, Bulk Enrichment, New Modules and More — Optional

Silent Push 6.0 has launched with an MCP Server for querying the platform from AI tools, bulk enrichment for up to 100 domains or IPs, rebuilt TLP Amber reports, and a reorganized module structure.

  • Silent Push announced Silent Push 6.0 as its biggest release yet.
  • The MCP Server lets teams query Silent Push from Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT, or any AI tool already in their workflow.
  • Bulk Enrichment handles up to 100 domains or IPs at once in the Insight module.
  • TLP Amber reports have been fully rebuilt with pivotable indicators and a new API for programmatic access.
  • The Silent Push platform has been reorganised into four modules: Defend, Insight, Reconnaissance, and Advanced Attribution.

Top Chainguard alternatives 2026 — Optional

The article argues that Chainguard’s hardened container images are strong but require migration to its Wolfi-based catalog and ongoing digest updates, creating operational friction. It positions Aikido Security as the best alternative because it patches CVEs in existing base images and application dependencies without forcing a proprietary distro migration.

  • Chainguard provides hardened, near-zero CVE container images built on its Wolfi Linux distribution, with signed SBOMs, Sigstore signatures, nightly rebuilds, and published remediation timelines for vulnerabilities.
  • The article says teams look for Chainguard alternatives because adopting Chainguard requires moving to its curated catalog and distribution, and because patches arrive through new image digests that require ongoing testing and approval.
  • Aikido Security is presented as the strongest alternative because it patches vulnerabilities in existing container base images and application dependencies without requiring migration to a proprietary distribution.
  • The article identifies Docker Hardened Images, Minimus, RapidFort, and Echo as direct alternatives for teams that mainly want hardened container images.
  • RapidFort, Echo, Minimus, and Docker Hardened Images are described as more narrowly focused on hardened images, while Aikido is described as covering broader software security functions such as code scanning, dependency scanning, infrastructure checks, secrets detection, cloud posture management, and runtime protection.

Webinar tomorrow: Why modern email attacks require a new approach to defense — Optional

BleepingComputer is hosting a webinar on July 8 about using behavioral AI to detect and automate responses to modern email threats like phishing, BEC, device code phishing, and account takeover. The session focuses on reducing alert fatigue and improving defenses as attackers increasingly abuse trusted identities and normal business workflows.

  • BleepingComputer will host a live webinar on July 8 titled “Stop chasing alerts: Automating email security with behavioral AI.”
  • The webinar will be presented by Dan Nickolaisen of Abnormal AI and Eric Danneker of Novant Health.
  • The article says phishing, business email compromise, and account takeover remain persistent threats despite investments in secure email gateways, multi-factor authentication, and identity protection.
  • The webinar will examine how behavioral AI can identify abnormal communication patterns, automate investigations, and accelerate response efforts.
  • The webinar will cover topics including Device Code phishing, trusted sender impersonation, alert fatigue, manual investigations, and automated detection and remediation workflows.
